## Identity Lifecycle Management

**Parent L1**: Identity and Access Management
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Identity Lifecycle Management governs the full lifecycle of digital identities — from initial creation through modification, suspension, and permanent deprovisioning — for all identity populations: workforce, partner, customer, and non-human. It ensures that access rights reflect current employment, relationship, and role status at all times, eliminating the orphaned and over-privileged accounts that create persistent access risk. The capability encompasses joiner-mover-leaver processes, identity attribute governance, and authoritative source integration.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Govern and Protect functions; supports compliance with CMS identity management requirements and HIPAA access control obligations
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Identity that is not current, properly scoped, and traceable to an authoritative source cannot serve as a trustworthy Zero Trust control plane input; lifecycle discipline is the foundation on which all other IAM capabilities depend
**Key Stakeholders**: HR and workforce systems, application owners, identity platform teams, security governance
**Related ABBs**: GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01 (lifecycle management within composite scope)
**Capability Boundary**: This capability governs the existence and attributes of identities; what identities may do is governed by the Authorization capability; whether identities are who they claim to be at enrollment is governed by Identity Proofing and Assurance

## Identity Governance and Administration (IGA)

**Parent L1**: Identity and Access Management
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Identity Governance and Administration ensures that access rights remain appropriate, authorized, and consistent with business roles throughout the identity lifecycle. It encompasses periodic access certification campaigns, role definition and maintenance, entitlement management, and separation of duties (SoD) enforcement. IGA provides the structured oversight layer that detects access accumulation, role conflicts, and policy violations before they become audit findings or security incidents.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Govern and Identify functions; directly supports HIPAA minimum necessary access requirements and CMS access review obligations
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Continuous access review is the governance analog of continuous verification — it ensures that standing access rights reflect current need and authorization, preventing the accumulation of implicit trust through unchallenged entitlements
**Key Stakeholders**: Compliance and audit teams, application business owners, identity governance program, security operations
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-IAM-IGA-2.2.13](GUID-SEC-IAM-IGA-2.2.13.md) (draft)
**Capability Boundary**: IGA governs the appropriateness of access rights; granting and enforcement of those rights is the Authorization capability; the detection of access misuse at runtime is the Identity Monitoring and Analytics capability

## Authentication

**Parent L1**: Identity and Access Management
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Authentication is the capability that verifies a claimed identity at access time by requiring the presenting subject to demonstrate possession of, or binding to, one or more authenticators. The enterprise authentication capability spans the full NIST SP 800-63B Authenticator Assurance Level (AAL) spectrum — from basic single-factor for low-risk access to phishing-resistant hardware-bound authenticators for privileged and sensitive access. It includes adaptive authentication, risk-based step-up, and re-authentication for context changes.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AA — Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control); directly addresses the requirement to verify all users before granting access
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Authentication is the most direct realization of the Zero Trust principle "always verify" — no access may proceed without a current, context-appropriate authentication event; the AAL assigned to a session directly calibrates the degree of trust granted
**Key Stakeholders**: End users (all populations), platform engineers, application owners, identity platform teams, security architects
**Related ABBs**: GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04
**Capability Boundary**: Authentication establishes that a subject is who they claim to be; what that authenticated subject may access is determined by the Authorization capability; the conditions under which authentication is required or stepped up draw on signals from the Devices and Networks Zero Trust pillars

## Authorization

**Parent L1**: Identity and Access Management
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Authorization is the capability that governs what an authenticated identity may do — which resources it may access, what operations it may perform, and under what conditions. Enterprise authorization encompasses role-based access control (RBAC) for structured entitlement models, attribute-based access control (ABAC) for context-sensitive policy evaluation, and policy decision and enforcement points that evaluate access requests against current identity, device, resource, and environmental context. Authorization is the architectural mechanism through which Zero Trust access decisions are operationalized at runtime.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AA); supports minimum-necessary access requirements across HIPAA, CMS, and state Medicaid program obligations
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Authorization is the Zero Trust enforcement point — it is where the principle "assume breach, minimize blast radius" is operationalized through least-privilege, time-limited, and scope-constrained access grants
**Key Stakeholders**: Application architects, platform engineers, security architects, data owners, compliance teams
**Related ABBs**: GUID-SEC-IAM-AUTHZ-2.2.08 (draft)
**Capability Boundary**: Authorization governs access rights at runtime; defining which roles and entitlements should exist is the IGA capability; enforcing access at the network layer is the network security domain

## Identity Federation and Single Sign-On

**Parent L1**: Identity and Access Management
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Identity Federation and Single Sign-On is the capability that establishes, governs, and operates trust relationships between identity domains — enabling authenticated identity claims to flow across organizational and technical boundaries without requiring redundant authentication. It includes federation protocol mediation (SAML 2.0, OIDC), IdP hub-and-spoke topology management, external CSP integration, cross-domain attribute normalization, and SSO session lifecycle management. The capability serves all identity populations: workforce SSO across enterprise applications, partner federation, and customer identity across client-facing portals.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect; enables user experience consistency while maintaining security governance across federated trust relationships
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Federation must not introduce implicit trust; every federated assertion must be validated, scoped to the requesting application's needs, and subject to continuous verification within the consuming session — the federation capability implements the identity pillar of Zero Trust across domain boundaries
**Key Stakeholders**: Enterprise SSO users, partner organizations, application teams, identity platform teams, security architects
**Related ABBs**: GUID-SEC-IAM-IDENTITY-BROKER-2.2.02, GUID-SEC-IAM-SSO-2.2.03
**Capability Boundary**: This capability governs identity trust flows between domains; what federated identities may do within a domain is governed by Authorization; the assurance level of a federated identity is established by Identity Proofing and Assurance at the originating CSP

## Credential and Attribute Management

**Parent L1**: Identity and Access Management
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Credential and Attribute Management governs the lifecycle of authenticators and identity attributes — the raw material from which authentication and authorization decisions are constructed. It encompasses password policy and reset flows, certificate lifecycle management (issuance, renewal, revocation), API key and token management, identity attribute stores, attribute synchronization between authoritative sources and consuming applications, and secure credential storage. For non-human identities, it includes the vaulting and rotation of service account credentials.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect; credential compromise is among the highest-impact initial access vectors; effective credential lifecycle management directly reduces this risk surface
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Short-lived credentials, certificate-based binding, and automated rotation reduce the window of opportunity for credential misuse — each is a direct Zero Trust architectural pattern that limits the blast radius of credential compromise
**Key Stakeholders**: Identity platform teams, application developers, security operations, privileged access management teams
**Related ABBs**: GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01 (within composite scope), GUID-SEC-IAM-PAM-2.2.06 (for privileged credential vaulting)
**Capability Boundary**: Credential management governs authenticators and their lifecycle; the policy governing which credential types are acceptable for which assurance levels is the Authentication capability; management of secrets in application deployments is shared with the Non-Human and AI Identity Management capability

## Privileged Access Management

**Parent L1**: Identity and Access Management
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Privileged Access Management governs the lifecycle, use, and accountability of elevated access — administrative credentials, root accounts, service accounts with broad permissions, and any access that, if compromised, could have disproportionate impact on enterprise systems or data. PAM establishes zero standing privilege as an architectural target: privileged access is granted just-in-time, for defined scope and duration, with full session recording and post-use revocation. It encompasses credential vaulting, JIT provisioning workflows, tiered administration models, and break-glass emergency access.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect and Detect; privileged access misuse — whether by external attackers or insiders — is consistently the highest-impact access risk scenario; PAM is a primary risk reduction capability
**Zero Trust Relevance**: PAM is the most direct architectural realization of the Zero Trust principle that no identity — including administrators — should have implicit or persistent trust; every privileged action should be explicitly authorized, time-bound, and auditable
**Key Stakeholders**: Infrastructure and platform administrators, security operations, audit and compliance, incident response teams
**Related ABBs**: GUID-SEC-IAM-PAM-2.2.06
**Capability Boundary**: PAM governs elevated access to systems and infrastructure; authorization of standard application access is the Authorization capability; management of non-human service credentials that are not privileged is the Non-Human and AI Identity Management capability

## Identity Proofing and Assurance

**Parent L1**: Identity and Access Management
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Identity Proofing and Assurance is the capability that establishes the degree of confidence an enterprise has in a claimed identity at the point of enrollment — calibrated through the NIST SP 800-63A Identity Assurance Level (IAL) framework. It encompasses IAL determination based on risk assessment, evidence collection and validation, identity verification through authoritative sources and biometric comparison, fraud detection, and the governance of external Credential Service Providers (CSPs) such as ID.me for healthcare program enrollment scenarios. The established IAL becomes the calibration point for all subsequent authentication and authorization decisions for that identity.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Govern and Protect; healthcare program enrollment (Medicaid eligibility, provider enrollment) requires verified identity to prevent fraudulent access to program benefits
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Zero Trust requires that identity claims be verifiable and trustworthy; identity proofing is the process by which that trust is established at the source — an unproofed identity cannot serve as a reliable Zero Trust control plane input for sensitive access
**Key Stakeholders**: Medicaid program enrollment teams, provider relations, member services, security architects, fraud prevention
**Related ABBs**: GUID-SEC-IAM-PROOFING-2.2.05, GUID-SEC-IAM-ID.ME-STRATEGY-2.2.10
**Capability Boundary**: Proofing establishes identity assurance at enrollment; ongoing authentication strength is the Authentication capability; IGA governs whether an enrolled, proofed identity continues to hold appropriate access rights

[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-CAP-DESC-2.1.03.md#non-human-and-ai-identity-management]

## Non-Human and AI Identity Management

**Parent L1**: Identity and Access Management
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Non-Human and AI Identity Management governs the identities of automated systems — service accounts, API clients, containerized workloads, CI/CD pipelines, and AI/ML systems — applying the same Zero Trust rigor to non-human subjects that applies to human users. It encompasses service account lifecycle management, cryptographic workload identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE, platform managed identities), machine-to-machine authentication protocols (RFC 8705, RFC 9449), AI system access scoping by lifecycle phase, and behavioral monitoring for non-human identity anomalies. Agentic AI systems require specialized governance for delegation chains linking autonomous actions to authorizing human principals.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Govern and Protect; as automation and AI adoption grow, non-human identities increasingly represent the highest-volume and, if ungoverned, highest-risk identity population
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Non-human identities frequently bypass Zero Trust controls that are applied to human access because they operate programmatically and at high volume; this capability ensures no identity is exempt from cryptographic verification, least privilege, and continuous monitoring — regardless of whether the acting subject is human
**Key Stakeholders**: Platform engineers, DevSecOps teams, AI/ML platform teams, security architects, service account owners
**Related ABBs**: GUID-SEC-IAM-NON-HUMAN-AND-AI-STRATEGY-2.2.12
**Capability Boundary**: Non-human identity management governs the identities of automated systems; the Authorization capability governs what those identities may do; the Privileged Access Management capability governs service accounts that hold elevated or administrative permissions

## Identity Monitoring and Analytics

**Parent L1**: Identity and Access Management
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Identity Monitoring and Analytics is the capability that provides continuous visibility into identity-related events — authentication attempts, access grants and denials, privilege escalations, account changes, and behavioral deviations — across all identity populations. It establishes behavioral baselines, integrates with enterprise SIEM, and provides anomaly detection tuned to the distinct patterns of human, privileged, and non-human identities. Identity analytics translate raw event streams into threat detection signals that feed security operations workflows.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Detect (DE.AE — Adverse Event Analysis); identity event detection is the primary mechanism for identifying compromised credentials and insider access misuse
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Zero Trust requires continuous verification — not just at the moment of authentication; identity monitoring provides the runtime signal that enables continuous re-evaluation of trust assumptions, triggering step-up authentication or session revocation when behavioral context changes
**Key Stakeholders**: Security operations center, threat detection teams, identity platform teams, compliance and audit
**Related ABBs**: GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01 (monitoring within composite scope)
**Capability Boundary**: Identity monitoring consumes event data from all IAM capabilities; security incident investigation and response is the Security Operations capability; network-level behavioral analytics is the Network Security capability
